info.name: idempotency_lab
info.description:
HTTP idempotency lab (branch idem-api-HTTP-flow). Two parallel route trees over the same resources: /naive has no protection, /safe uses the mechanism that suits each method. Every mutation appends to audit_log, so GET /_stats shows whether a retry duplicated anything.

Start the lab (`make up && make run`), keep {{baseUrl}} at http://localhost:8080, then browse "1. Endpoints" by hand or run "2. Scenarios" in the Collection Runner.

item.name: 1. Endpoints
Lab controls

request.description: Scoreboard. Read it after a run: an idempotent endpoint leaves these counts flat after the first call.
Truncate users, information, audit_log and idempotency_keys.
Delete expired idempotency keys (batched, 10000 rows). Production runs this on a schedule.
Lab-only: make every key look expired, to test the TTL boundary without waiting 24h.
The generated Swagger 2.0 spec. The UI is at {{baseUrl}}/swagger/index.html.

item.description: Scoreboard, reset, and TTL controls. Mounted at the root, no /naive or /safe prefix.

item.name: Users - naive

request.description: List live users.
Read one user. Saves the ETag into {{etag}}. Send it as If-None-Match to get 304.
Create a user with no protection. Every send creates another row. Saves the id into {{userId}}.
Upsert that still bumps version and appends an audit row on every identical call.
Accumulating patch: name = name || append_name. Each send changes the state again.
Hard delete. Audits on every call, even when nothing was deleted.

item.description: No protection anywhere. The control group.

item.name: Users - safe

request.description: List live users.
Read one user. Saves the ETag into {{etag}}. Send it as If-None-Match to get 304.

Same handler as /naive, behind the Idempotency-Key middleware. Resend with the same {{idemKey}} to get the stored response replayed (Idempotent-Replayed: true). Change the body with the same key to get 422. Saves the id into {{userId}}.
Assignment guarded by a content hash: 201 on create, 200 on replace, version unchanged on an identical write. Optional If-Match / If-None-Match: *.
JSON Merge Patch with a mandatory If-Match. Run GET /safe/users/:id first so {{etag}} is current. Without If-Match: 428. Stale ETag: 412.
Guarded soft delete: 204 the first time, 410 after that (tombstone), 404 if it never existed.

item.description: Each method protected by the mechanism that suits it. POST needs an Idempotency-Key because users have no naturally unique field.

item.name: Information - naive

request.description: List live information records.
Read one record. Saves the ETag into {{infoEtag}}.
The unique phone index still blocks a duplicate, but the second send gets a 500 that leaks the constraint name. Saves the id into {{infoId}}.
age = age + age_increment. Every retry ages the person again.
Hard delete, audits on every call.

item.description: No protection. There is no naive PUT: a two-field replacement is idempotent almost by accident.

item.name: Information - safe

request.description: List live information records.
Read one record. Saves the ETag into {{infoEtag}}.
No Idempotency-Key needed: the unique phone index is the dedup. A repeat returns 200 with the existing record and Idempotent-Replayed: true. Saves the id into {{infoId}}.
Full replacement at a client-known URI: 201 on create, 200 on replace. 409 if the phone belongs to another record.
Merge patch with absolute values and a mandatory If-Match. Run GET /safe/information/:id first so {{infoEtag}} is current.
Guarded soft delete: 204, then 410.

item.description: information has a unique phone, so a UNIQUE index gives POST idempotency for free.

Every route of the lab, one request each, for poking at by hand. Requests share collection variables: create something first (POST) and the id lands in {{userId}} / {{infoId}}; a GET stores the ETag for the PATCH requests.

item.name: 2. Scenarios
01 POST without protection duplicates

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.description: A client sends the same POST three times, e.g. after timeouts. The server picks the id, so every attempt creates another user.

item.name: 02 Idempotency-Key replays the first response

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("same id as the first attempt", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("firstUserId")));
pm.test("same id as the first attempt", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("firstUserId")));

item.name: Check: one user, one audit row

item.description: Same three attempts, now with one Idempotency-Key. The first runs the handler and stores a receipt in the same transaction; the retries get that stored response back.

item.name: 03 Same key, different body is rejected

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.name: Reuse the key for different content

exec: pm.test("users_live = 1  (the mismatched request did not run)", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().users_live).to.eql(1));

item.description: The middleware fingerprints sha256(method, path, body). Same key with a different body is a client bug, not a retry, so it gets 422 instead of someone else's response.

item.name: 04 Keys are scoped per tenant

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.name: Tenant demo creates with key K
Tenant other-tenant sends the same key K

exec: pm.test("a NEW id, not tenant demo's response", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("firstUserId")));
pm.test("idempotency_keys = 2  (one key row per (tenant, endpoint, key))", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().idempotency_keys).to.eql(2));

item.description: Keys are unique per (X-Api-Key, endpoint, key). Without that scope, tenant B could replay tenant A's response body.

item.name: 05 Crash after the write: rollback vs duplicate

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("users_live = 2  (the 500 had already committed a row)", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().users_live).to.eql(2));

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.name: Check safe: nothing committed, key released

item.description: X-Chaos: fail-after-write returns 500 after the insert. On /naive the row already autocommitted, so the retry duplicates it. On /safe the insert and the receipt share one transaction: the 500 rolls both back and releases the key.

item.name: 06 PUT: assignment should be a no-op after the first

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.
Only generates {{putId}}; the response is not used.
Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("audit_entries = 1  (only the real change is audited)", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().audit_entries).to.eql(1));

item.description: PUT is idempotent because it is an assignment. The naive upsert still bumps version and audits every call; the safe one compares a content hash. Note 201 then 200: different status codes, identical server state.

item.name: 07 PATCH: accumulation vs assignment

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("age = 33 -- depends on how many retries happened", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().age).to.eql(33));

item.description: age = age + n depends on how many times it ran. {"age": 31} gives the same result every time; If-Match adds concurrency control on top. A retry that reuses the current ETag succeeds as a true no-op because an identical patch does not advance the version.

item.name: 08 Unique constraint dedups POST without a key table

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.
Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("same id as the first attempt", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("firstInfoId")));

item.description: information.phone has a UNIQUE index, so the database refuses the duplicate either way. Naive surfaces it as a 500; safe catches 23505 and returns the existing record with 200.

item.name: 09 DELETE: side effect once, then 410

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("audit_entries = 4  (1 create + 3 deletes for one deletion)", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().audit_entries).to.eql(4));

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.description: The postcondition of DELETE is absence. Naive hard-deletes and audits every call; safe soft-deletes behind a guard, so retries get 410 (you already did this) rather than 404 (never existed).

item.name: 10 Conditional GET with ETag

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

item.description: GET is safe and idempotent by construction. The version-backed ETag lets a client revalidate cheaply with 304 Not Modified.

item.name: 11 After the TTL a retry is a new operation

request.description: Truncate every table so this scenario starts from zero.

exec: pm.test("users_live = 2  (the receipt was gone, so the retry ran again)", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().users_live).to.eql(2));

item.description: Receipts live for 24h. Once a key is swept, the same key is treated as a brand-new request -- which is why the TTL has to be documented for clients.

Runnable experiments. Each scenario folder starts with POST /_reset and asserts the outcome with tests, so you can run a single scenario (or all of them) with the Collection Runner and read the test results. Concurrent retries (409 + Retry-After) cannot be reproduced by the sequential runner; `make test` covers that case with parallel curl.
